findings.text: Provides per-CPU deferred work polling and draining with synchronous wait. Callers query pending status before idle transitions, invoke drain helpers from interrupt or tick context, and wait for a specific item from sleepable context with interrupts enabled.

An item becomes reusable after its pending mark clears under ownership without atomic operations, while its busy mark clears only when no concurrent claimant intervened. Completion wakes waiters when running without architected interrupt signalling or for non-hard items under fully preemptible operation.

Raised work drains promptly on explicit run and on tick when no architected signal exists. Lazy work drains together with raised work in classic operation but is delegated to a per-CPU thread wakeup under fully preemptible operation, with the thread draining only the lazy list under read-side protection.

Registers a per-CPU thread for lazy work that runs at low FIFO priority, executes when its should-run predicate holds, and performs the lazy-list drain routine. Registration occurs once during early init and only in fully preemptible builds.

Going offline with queued items triggers a one-time warning, since all work is expected flushed beforehand. Draining requires interrupts disabled in classic builds, so invocation from enabled-interrupt context is a programming error.

Exposes cross-task resource identity comparison keyed by caller PID namespace identifiers and a type selector. Supported selectors cover files, address spaces, file tables, filesystem state, signal handling state, I/O context, System V semaphore undo state where built, and epoll membership; unknown selectors fail as invalid and unsupported builds fail as not supported.

Raw kernel pointer values never leave the interface directly. Each compared address is mixed with a per-type secret pair initialized once from random bytes with forced oddness and high-bit set, then ordered numerically with a three-valued encoding distinguishing less, equal and greater.

Both target tasks have their execution-update read locks held during inspection and permission checks. Acquisition orders the two locks by address to avoid deadlock, uses killable waits, treats identical locks singly, and releases in the complementary order.

Tasks resolve under read-side protection with reference holds before locks are taken. Missing tasks report as nonexistent, inadequate ptrace read rights report as permission denied, absent file descriptors report as bad descriptor, and user memory faults report as fault.

Central coverage object holds a reference count, a guarding spin lock, a mode, a buffer length in words, a shared buffer pointer, an owning task pointer, a remote-collection flag, a remote area length, and a re-enable sequence number. Mode, length, buffer and owning task change only under the spin lock.

Remote tracking uses a handle-to-object entry with hash linkage, a reusable area descriptor with list linkage and length, two global free lists distinguished by interrupt context, a global spin lock for the handle table, and per-CPU local locking for collection safety.

The object spin lock with interrupt save serializes mode transitions, buffer installation, mapping validation and local enable or disable. The separate remote table lock serializes handle registration during remote enable and is dropped before any failure unwind that disables collection.

Lifecycle moves from disabled to initialized after buffer setup, then to program-counter or comparison tracing after enable for the current task, returning to disabled on explicit disable or task exit with reference accounting. Remote enable additionally records remote sizing and handle set and marks the task as a remote collector.

Handles authenticate by subsystem and instance masks with distinct validity for common, zero and uncommon classes. Duplicate registration fails as already present, allocation failure fails as out of memory, and reusable areas match by exact length within the same interrupt class.

Compiler-inserted hooks record return addresses and integer comparison operands into the current task buffer when tracing of the matching kind is active. Width-specific and constant-aware variants funnel into a common recorder, and switch handling expands multi-way branches into repeated comparison records with size-derived typing.

Buffers share a leading count word followed by payload slots with strict capacity checks that silently drop overflow. Program-counter entries store normalized addresses; comparison entries store type, two operands and normalized site. Count updates precede payload stores with ordering to tolerate reentrant interrupt records.
Each comparison record occupies four 64-bit words in the shared buffer.

Offers device-style open, mapping, control and close. Open allocates and initializes a fresh object in disabled state with unit reference; mapping exposes the exact buffer range without expansion; close drops a reference; control validates sizes, modes and handle vectors before state changes.

Undersized or oversized buffer requests, mapping with nonzero offset or mismatched length, control without prior initialization, double use by distinct tasks, nonzero reserved arguments, handle count beyond the maximum, and mismatched user copies all fail safely without state change. Page insertion failure emits a single warning.

Waiting requires sleepable context and is valid only for items that signal completion via wait queue; those paths block uninterruptibly until busy clears and then observe a grace period so no post-completion access occurs. Architected-interrupt builds instead spin briefly on the busy mark.

List draining assumes exclusion via disabled interrupts in classic builds and relies on atomic list handover to detach all entries at once. Thread-based lazy draining additionally holds read-side protection across the drain, while synchronous waiting pairs queue wakeup with a grace period for safe reclamation.
Diagnostics from this component carry a fixed identifying prefix, and its own code is excluded from branch profiling instrumentation.
